summary: Redefines the meaning of the two data link layer codepoints that RFC 3032 set up to tell MPLS unicast from MPLS multicast. The original multicast distinction was never deployed, so both codepoints can now carry multicast packets, and the second keeps its role for upstream-assigned labels. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023.

plainLanguage.summary: There were two doors on a building, one for singles and one for groups, but nobody used the group door. This repurposes both so either can carry group deliveries.

questions: what is the mpls multicast codepoint
subtitle: Repurposes the two MPLS Ethernet codepoints so both can carry multicast, and says what MAC address multicast MPLS frames use.

tldr.problem: RFC 3032 set up one codepoint for MPLS unicast and one for MPLS multicast, but the multicast codepoint was never deployed and does not capture how multicast MPLS actually works. RFC 3032 also never said which MAC destination address an Ethernet multicast MPLS frame should use.
tldr.mechanism: The two codepoints are redefined: the first carries MPLS packets in general, and the second means the top label is upstream-assigned. The RFC also specifies the encapsulation rules for Ethernet, PPP, GRE and IP, and a MAC destination address format of 01-00-5e-8v-wx-yz.
tldr.outcome: Implementations of the old multicast codepoint use cannot interoperate with ones that follow this document, but the RFC says the old use was never deployed with a control plane. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023.

today: RFC 5332 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why the Codepoints Needed Redefining
sections.content:
RFC 3032 established two data link layer codepoints for MPLS: one to say a frame carries an MPLS unicast packet, and one to say it carries an MPLS multicast packet. The term "multicast packet" was never precisely defined. This RFC says the multicast codepoint has never been deployed, and later work on MPLS multicast showed that two codepoints are needed but that RFC 3032 does not describe their use properly.

The RFC defines a multicast label as one whose Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) in a given context names a set of next hops, with the meaning that the packet is replicated and a copy sent to each one. A set with a single member still counts. The receiver learns this from its own NHLFE lookup, so the codepoint does not need to say it.

The old use of the multicast codepoint, as specified in RFC 3032 and RFC 4023, is deprecated. The RFC warns that an implementation that does MPLS multicast the old way cannot interoperate with one that follows this document. It argues this is not a practical problem: platforms using the old codepoint lack the control plane for MPLS multicast, so they would not try to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said one door was for groups, but the building already knew which packages were for groups. So the doors were given new jobs instead.

sections.title: Upstream-Assigned and Downstream-Assigned Labels
sections.content:
Suppose router R1 sends a labeled packet to router R2 with label L, and R2 must look up L to find the matching Forwarding Equivalence Class. If R2 made the binding between L and that class and told R1, the label is downstream-assigned. RFC 3031 only discusses this kind.

If R1 made the binding and told R2, the label is upstream-assigned. A label bound by a third party, R3, and advertised to both R1 and R2 also counts as upstream-assigned. Upstream-assigned labels need not come from the same label space as downstream-assigned ones; the procedures for interpreting them are in RFC 5331.

Using upstream-assigned labels is an OPTIONAL feature, and multicast labels MAY be upstream-assigned under the conditions the RFC gives. They MUST NOT be used unless it is known that the downstream router supports them. How that is known is out of scope. The RFC makes no changes to unicast label procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a coat check. Usually the person at the receiving end hands out the ticket numbers. Sometimes the sender picks the number instead, and the receiver has to know which way it is being done.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Link or Tunnel
sections.content:
An MPLS packet travels over a data link, an MPLS tunnel, or an IP tunnel. In every case the receiving router must know whether the top label is upstream-assigned or downstream-assigned. The RFC sorts links and tunnels into three types.

  • Point-to-point: in each direction, either every packet carries an upstream-assigned label or every packet carries a downstream-assigned one. Without other information, downstream-assigned MUST be presumed.
  • Point-to-multipoint: only one system can transmit, and the top labels of all packets on the link MUST be of the same type. The receivers must know in advance which type it is.
  • Multipoint-to-multipoint: any system can transmit. Either all top labels are known to be downstream-assigned, or all are known to be upstream-assigned, or the two kinds are mixed.

Only in the mixed case, the encapsulation MUST provide a codepoint saying which kind the top label is. If a link or tunnel type has no such codepoint, the mixed case MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: On a private line between two friends, everybody knows the rules. On a big party line, you need a sticker on each message if the rules can differ from message to message.

sections.title: Codepoints for Ethernet, PPP, GRE and IP
sections.content:
On Ethernet, ethertype 0x8847 is used for any unicast frame carrying MPLS. It is also used for multicast frames, except when the top label is upstream-assigned. Ethertype 0x8848, formerly the "MPLS multicast codepoint", is used only when an MPLS packet with an upstream-assigned top label is carried in a multicast Ethernet frame.

On PPP, a point-to-point link, the Protocol field is always 0x0281 for MPLS.

For GRE, RFC 4023 is modified. If the GRE destination IP address is unicast, 0x8847 MUST be used in all cases. If it is multicast, 0x8847 MUST be used for a downstream-assigned top label and 0x8848 MUST be used for an upstream-assigned one. If it is known by other means that a multicast-addressed GRE packet carries an upstream-assigned label, seeing 0x8847 there is an error and the packet MUST be discarded.

For MPLS in IP, the IPv4 Protocol Number or IPv6 Next Header field is always 137, whether or not the packet is multicast. With a multicast IP destination, the tunnel is treated as point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint, and all its packets have the same label type at the top of the stack. How that is determined is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of road has its own sign for MPLS traffic. Ethernet has two signs, one for ordinary labels and one for labels the sender picked. The other roads mostly use a single sign.

sections.title: The Ethernet MAC Destination Address
sections.content:
RFC 3032 allows an MPLS packet in an Ethernet multicast frame but never said how to set the MAC Destination Address (MAC DA). This RFC says a router sending multicast MPLS in a multicast frame MUST set it to 01-00-5e-8v-wx-yz, where vwxyz is a 20-bit (five-nibble) value. It MAY be set to 0, or it MAY be set to the value of one of the MPLS labels on the stack. Which is the default is implementation-dependent.

Routers using the two choices MUST interoperate: a router MUST NOT filter packets whose vwxyz is zero, and MUST NOT indiscriminately filter all packets where it is non-zero. When copying a label and the stack has two or more labels, the default is the second label, the entry right after the top one, though a router MAY be configured to use another. With only one label, that label is used.

The RFC expects routers to follow RFC 5331, pushing a top "context label" that is the same for every packet the router sends onto the Ethernet, with a second label that differs per LSP. Basing the address on the second label puts more LSP-specific information into the MAC DA, which can be used to filter packets with unexpected non-zero values. Broadcast addresses are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The delivery address on the envelope has a few blank spots. You can leave them as zero or copy in a number from the package label. Either way, the mail room must not throw the envelope away just because of which one you chose.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA already owns the Ethernet multicast addresses from 01-00-5e-00-00-00 to 01-00-5e-ff-ff-ff. The lower half, up to 01-00-5e-7f-ff-ff, was already reserved for IP multicast in Ethernet multicast frames.

IANA reserved 01-00-5e-80-00-00 to 01-00-5e-8f-ff-ff for MPLS multicast packets in Ethernet multicast frames. These addresses are valid with ethertype 8847 or 8848. IANA also changed the ethertype descriptions: 8847 is "MPLS", as defined in RFC 3032 and this document, and 8848 is "MPLS with upstream-assigned label".
sections.plainLanguage: A part of the address book was set aside just for this kind of mail, and the two door labels were renamed to match their new jobs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3032 and RFC 4023 apply. Maliciously changing the codepoint may cause packets to be lost or misrouted, although changing the codepoint without also changing the label has no predictable effect.

Maliciously altering the MAC DA on an Ethernet can cause packets to be received by a third party instead of the intended recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad actor changes the door sign or the address on the envelope, the package can get lost or end up with the wrong person.
